# Paper 1 - Structured Findings Summary

*Generated by `src/s07_documents.py` from `analysis/models/results_registry.csv` and `tests_registry.csv`. Coefficients are reported
as per cent changes in the wholesale price (100 x coefficient on ln price); standard errors are clustered by district (64 clusters).*

## Headline

In a panel of 34,341 market x commodity x month observations (2000-01 to 2026-08), **local pre-harvest weather shocks have no detectable
effect on local wholesale onion and potato prices.** The estimate is small and tightly bounded, the old placebo failure is resolved,
and the one shock type with a significant coefficient (heat) does not survive its own placebo test. H1-H4 are not supported.

| Hypothesis | Verdict | Key evidence |
|---|---|---|
| H1: adverse pre-harvest shocks raise prices | **Not supported** | -0.14% (SE 0.17, p = 0.423) per shocked month |
| H2: response within 1-3 months, gone by 4-6 | **Not supported** | no lag individually robust; all lags jointly p = 0.107 (corrected event study) |
| H3: onion more sensitive than potato | **Not supported** | onion - potato difference +0.17% (SE 0.36, p = 0.638) |
| H4: larger response farther from Dhaka | **Not supported** | interaction with ln distance +0.21% (SE 0.21, p = 0.308) |

## Key Result 1 - Overall effect of pre-harvest shocks

* Model 1 (market x commodity FE, commodity x year-month FE): one more shocked month in the pre-harvest window changes the wholesale
  price over the following marketing year by **-0.14% (SE 0.17, p = 0.423)**; 95% CI [-0.47%, +0.20%].
* Alternative inference: HC1 SE 0.11; two-way (district, year-month) SE 0.22 (p = 0.547).
* Within R2 = 0.0001 (overall R2 0.965 is almost entirely fixed effects).
* With market-specific linear trends: -0.12% (SE 0.18, p = 0.493).
* Power: with this standard error the design detects effects of about 0.47% per shocked month (80% power, 5% level). The mean
  exposure is 1.07 shocked months (SD 0.96), so a one-SD change in exposure moves prices by at most
  about 0.45% in absolute value at the edge of the confidence interval. This is an informative null,
  not an underpowered one.

## Key Result 2 - Shock types

| Shock type (months in window) | Effect per month | Share of obs. with any |
|---|---|---|
| Excess rain (z > 1.5) | -0.22% (SE 0.25, p = 0.377) | 0.382 |
| Drought (z < -1.5) | +1.31% (SE 1.03, p = 0.207) | 0.007 |
| Heat (z > 1.5) | +0.85% (SE 0.32, p = 0.011) | 0.333 |
| Cold (z < -1.5) | -0.31% (SE 0.57, p = 0.585) | 0.239 |

Joint test that all four are zero: F = 3.25, p = 0.017.

**Heat is the only type with a significant coefficient, and it should not be read as causal:**

* Imported onion - which is not grown locally - shows a *larger* heat coefficient in the same districts: +1.77% (SE 0.66, p = 0.010).
* It is not monotone in the threshold: -0.13% (SE 0.23, p = 0.586) at 1.0 SD, +1.07% (SE 0.60, p = 0.078) at 2.0 SD.
* Next season's heat months carry a coefficient of the same size as the realised one in the clean-month sample
  (+0.64% (SE 0.46, p = 0.166) versus +0.60% (SE 0.40, p = 0.140)).
* It weakens with market-specific seasonality absorbed (+0.63% (SE 0.34, p = 0.069)) and in the STRICT tier (+0.72% (SE 0.38, p = 0.064)).
* Four shock types are tested; the Bonferroni-adjusted p-value of the baseline heat coefficient is 0.043.

**Drought is essentially untestable in this setting.** November-March rainfall normals are close to zero, so a -1.5 SD rainfall
anomaly is arithmetically impossible in those months; drought shocks can only occur in October, and only
0.7% of observations have any. The large CHIRPS drought coefficient in the robustness table rests on
0.04% of observations and is not interpretable.

## Key Result 3 - Onion versus potato

* Onion: -0.04% (SE 0.22, p = 0.864) (N = 11,977). Potato: -0.21% (SE 0.26, p = 0.423) (N = 22,364).
* Pooled interaction (onion minus potato): +0.17% (SE 0.36, p = 0.638). No evidence that the less storable crop is more sensitive.

## Key Result 4 - Spatial friction

* Shocked months x ln(distance to Dhaka, centred): +0.21% (SE 0.21, p = 0.308). Doubling distance changes the effect by
  +0.15 percentage points - economically negligible.
* Distance quartiles (Figure 5): -0.29% (SE 0.31, p = 0.353), -0.18% (SE 0.28, p = 0.528), -0.53% (SE 0.34, p = 0.128), +0.40% (SE 0.32, p = 0.211). No monotone gradient.
* Caveat: distance is measured from district centroids (market geocodes are not in the DAM data), and is geodesic rather than road distance.

## Key Result 5 - Event-study dynamics and the pre-trend test

The monthly event study regresses ln price on indicators for an in-window shock month in the district k months earlier (lags 0-6)
or later (leads 1-3, which should be zero).

| Specification | Joint test of leads (p) | All lags = 0 (p) | Cumulative effect, lags 0-6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) FE exactly as in the brief | **0.010 - fails** | 0.001 | +0.38% (p = 0.780) |
| (b) market x commodity x calendar-month FE | 0.738 - passes | 0.107 | -1.84% (p = 0.223) |
| (c) brief FE + district x crop x calendar-month FE | 0.575 - passes | 0.220 | -1.54% (p = 0.292) |

* **The pre-trend test fails under the fixed effects specified in the brief** (lead 1: -1.31% (SE 0.38, p = 0.001)). This is reported, not hidden.
* **Diagnosis.** The failure is not removed by market-specific trends (lead 1: -1.07% (SE 0.39, p = 0.008)), by district x crop x
  season FE (-1.21% (SE 0.49, p = 0.017)) or by controlling for continuous contemporaneous anomalies
  (-1.29% (SE 0.38, p = 0.001)), and the shock indicator is barely persistent (first-order autocorrelation 0.08).
  It is market-specific seasonality:
  market x commodity FE do not absorb the fact that harvest-season price troughs differ across markets, and in-window shocks by
  construction fall only in October-March. Once market x calendar-month effects are absorbed the leads are flat (p = 0.738).
* **Corrected estimates.** The only individually significant coefficient is one month after the shock (-1.17% (SE 0.53, p = 0.032)), a
  *fall*, driven by potato (-1.89% (SE 0.66, p = 0.006); onion -0.12% (SE 0.68, p = 0.861)). With ten coefficients
  estimated it would not survive a multiple-testing correction, and the lags are jointly insignificant in the pooled sample. A short-lived local
  dip is consistent with distress harvesting after rain or cold, but the evidence is suggestive at most.
* The season-level exposure of Models 1-4 is constant within a marketing year and therefore orthogonal to seasonality by construction;
  adding the seasonal FE to Model 1 gives -0.17% (SE 0.18, p = 0.362).
* Marketing-year dynamics (effect by quarter since the start of the marketing year): +0.24% (SE 0.22, p = 0.276), -0.02% (SE 0.23, p = 0.922), -0.60% (SE 0.25, p = 0.021), -0.28% (SE 0.32, p = 0.398);
  joint p = 0.075.

## Key Result 6 - Retail pass-through

* Elasticity of retail to wholesale price within market and month: **0.704** (SE 0.013; N = 23,948; within R2 0.700).
  Pass-through is incomplete in proportional terms, as expected when retail margins contain fixed per-kg costs.
* Conditional on the wholesale price, shocks do not move retail prices (+0.08% (SE 0.12, p = 0.520)); reduced form on retail
  +0.21% (SE 0.19, p = 0.273); on the retail-wholesale log margin +0.03% (SE 0.14, p = 0.848).

| Event-study leads, FE as in brief | p = 0.010 | **Fails** - see Key Result 5 |
| Event-study leads, seasonality absorbed | p = 0.738 | Passes |

with district clustering; coefficients range from -0.30% to +0.85%. The first-difference

**What survives:** the null for the aggregate exposure (every sample, threshold, weather source, clustering choice and trend specification);
the absence of onion/potato and distance heterogeneity; the pass-through elasticity.
**What is fragile:** the heat coefficient (fails the imported-onion placebo); the inverted-U in the quadratic model
(+1.50% (SE 0.52, p = 0.005); squared term -0.60% (SE 0.18, p = 0.001)) - the bin dummies that impose no functional form are jointly
insignificant (p = 0.182); the first-difference estimate; the one-month-lag dip for potato.

## Comparison with Letta, Montalbano & Pierre (2022) and the wider literature

* Letta et al. study Indian district wholesale prices and report that drought during the growing season raises food prices *before*
  harvest, which they interpret as traders' expectations. We find no comparable response in Bangladesh for onion and potato. We do not
  quote their magnitudes here because the published paper was not available in this environment; they must be checked against the article
  before the comparison is written up.
* Three differences make a like-for-like comparison difficult and probably explain much of the gap: (i) the Indian evidence is driven by
  drought in rain-fed kharif cereals and pulses, whereas onion and potato in Bangladesh are irrigated dry-season crops for which rainfall
  deficits are both rare and hard to define (see Key Result 2); (ii) Bangladesh is small and its vegetable markets are closely connected, so
  a district-level shock is diluted by trade, and anything national is absorbed by the commodity x month fixed effects; (iii) onion prices in
  Bangladesh are dominated by import policy shocks (the 2019-20 spike follows India's export ban), which are national.
* The result is in line with the Dell, Jones & Olken (2014) caution that panel weather designs identify *local, relative* effects: a zero here
  does not say weather is irrelevant for prices, only that local anomalies do not generate local price differentials.
* The agronomic literature (e.g. Auffhammer & Schlenker 2014; Burke & Lobell 2017; Guiteras 2009) finds yield losses from heat; our heat
  coefficient has the expected sign but fails the placebo, so we cannot attribute it to local crop damage.

## Limitations

1. **No time-varying controls at the district level.** Monthly customs imports, district cold-storage capacity, the BBS food CPI and BBS
   district production could not be obtained. National series (exchange rate, CPI) are collinear with the commodity x month fixed effects and
   enter only the less-saturated specification R18.
2. **Sample size is about 34,341, not the 100,000+ anticipated in the brief.** The expanded DAM file holds 126,932 rows across 13
   commodities and three price types; Paper 1's wholesale onion and potato series amount to 42,748 market-commodity-months.
3. **Markets are effectively district towns** (220 markets in 64 districts), and the 2025-26 API markets cannot be linked to the historical
   market names, so they enter as separate units.
4. **Reporting gaps**: 2014-10 to 2015-02, 2015-09 to 2015-12 and 2023-08 to 2025-05 (which includes all of 2024). Nothing is interpolated.
5. **Weather**: ERA5-Land precipitation was not available without a Copernicus key; ERA5 precipitation (the forcing from which ERA5-Land
   precipitation is interpolated) is used instead, with CHIRPS as the cross-check.
6. **External validity of a relative-price design**: effects of nationwide weather shocks on the national price level are not identified.
7. The forensic audit file `PAPER_1_PRE_HARVEST_SHOCKS/reports/PROJECT_STATE_AUDIT.md` is not in the repository (the folder is an empty
   submodule pointer), so the self-audit was done against the defects listed in the project brief.
